h: Irritation on the FICCI stage: corporate India drifts away from Modi
dek: In The Wire, Harish Khare writes that the scolding handed to industrialists on 19 November is a sign of a crack in the relationship on which Modi's entire politics was built.
body: Harish Khare, former editor-in-chief of The Tribune, recalls that a few months ago the Prime Minister's '25 years of public service' was celebrated, with the message that this leader sees business people as partners in progress. Then on 19 November, from the FICCI stage, the same leader was seen scolding industrialists for always asking for concessions.

According to the writer, historians may well see this day as the turning point when Modi's political model began to fall apart. Companies run for profit, not for a national project like 'Make in India', and since 1991 Indian business houses have become tied to global capital. Capital has no sentiment, but Modi treats everything as a personal relationship.

Modi sees himself as the guardian of the corporate world, while the rich see themselves as his sponsors. The writer gives the Nano project at Sanand as an example of corporate greed meeting a leader's ego.

The sharpest point is about wages. The Prime Minister chided industry for not raising pay, while in Noida the police cracked down on those asking for better wages and union activists were locked up under the National Security Act. Unions were weakened to make business easier, so in the writer's view the surprise at wages that have stood still for twenty-five years is an act.

The industrialists who gave money through electoral bonds, stitched together alliances and got parties split know how the leader's image was built, so they cannot be threatened. Without offering proof, Khare also hints that help in manufacturing a majority came from the Election Commission's office, and says the business class is the first to sense when a government's standing is slipping. In his opinion the days ahead will not be easy for the government.
nazar: In this squabble between power and big capital, the least space is left for the worker the Prime Minister spoke about from the stage. When Noida's workers took to the streets with exactly this demand, they got jail. Advice to raise wages will be believable only when the right to form unions, bargain and strike is given back.

Business drifting away from the government is not in itself a win for democracy. The real question is when the public will see the accounts of the relationship built on election donations and bargaining over policy.
sawal: Jail for Noida's workers, and a lecture on wages from the stage?
ref: FICCI
The Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, set up in 1927, the country's oldest body of industrialists, which talks to the government on policy.
Electoral bonds
A scheme for anonymous political donations started in 2018, which the Supreme Court struck down as unconstitutional in February 2024; the BJP received the most money.

h: The encounter habit crosses the border: the lesson of the Pannun plot
dek: In National Herald, Aakar Patel writes that Nikhil Gupta's 19-year sentence in the US shows that a country that accepts killing without trial at home takes the same habit abroad.
body: Aakar Patel's basic point is that 'encounters', meaning killings at the hands of the state, go on unchecked in India because there is no rule of law here. He mentions a former MP who had asked the Supreme Court for protection and was still shot dead in police custody in front of cameras. According to him, when the state lacks the ethics and the ability to investigate and prosecute lawfully, encounters become routine.

It is in this light that he sees the plot to kill Khalistan supporter Gurpatwant Singh Pannun. According to the charges of the US Justice Department, Vikash Yadav, posted in the Cabinet Secretariat, gave Nikhil Gupta the job of finding a killer in New York. A deal of about Rs 1 crore was fixed and an advance of nearly Rs 15 lakh in cash was paid on 9 June 2023, but the man who was paid turned out to be an undercover agent of a US agency.

The indictment contains audio, video and messages: photos in uniform, Pannun's address and daily routine, a promise to get a plane carrying drugs cleared out of Imphal airport, and an instruction to hold off the job around the Prime Minister's US visit of 21 to 23 June. It is also alleged that a photo of the body was sent the day after Hardeep Singh Nijjar was killed in Canada. Gupta was arrested in Prague on 30 June, pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 19 years in prison.

For Patel this is a failure not only of ethics but also of competence, because the US knew of the plot from the start. The government refused to share information, called the charges 'a matter of concern' and against its own policy, and hid behind a high-level committee. The writer expects that some Indians will be ashamed, while some who call themselves nationalists will even applaud the audacity. What was seen in the Manhattan court was not the intelligence agency of spy films.
nazar: A society that applauds encounters slowly comes to believe that courts and evidence are a waste of time. Among the families whose sons were killed in 'encounters', a large number are poor, Dalit and Muslim, and for them the road to justice is the longest.

The answer to charges against an Indian official abroad should be an open and independent inquiry, not silence. At home too, only a judicial inquiry into every encounter and prosecution of the officers responsible can break this habit.
sawal: The middleman was caught in Prague; who will answer in Delhi?
ref: The Nikhil Gupta case
A trial in the US in which Indian citizen Nikhil Gupta was charged with plotting to kill Sikh separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York; he pleaded guilty.
Encounter
A death in an alleged armed clash with the police or security forces; human rights groups have long said that a large number of these are fake.

h: App workers: no factory gate, no union flag
dek: In National Herald, Jagdish Rattanani writes that while crackdowns on workers' movements have grown, gig workers are building a new kind of power by turning the log-off into a strike, and Telangana's scheme is its first political echo.
body: Jagdish Rattanani, a journalist who teaches at SPJIMR, begins with the trade unions that have been weakening since liberalisation. According to him, under BJP rule the space for workers to make their voice heard has shrunk further. In April 2026, after a big strike in Noida's industrial area, more than 350 people demanding a higher minimum wage were arrested, including workers' representatives.

It is against this backdrop that the writer looks at gig workers. About 1.2 crore gig workers have been counted in the country, 4.2 lakh in Telangana alone, and the number could cross 2.3 crore by the end of the decade. On 14 November in Hyderabad, Rahul Gandhi and Chief Minister Revanth Reddy launched a scheme for them: accident insurance of five lakh rupees, health insurance of ten lakh, a welfare board funded by a one per cent fee on every transaction, transparency in data on work and payment, and rest spots in the city.

Rattanani says the platform companies are taking losses of more than Rs 12,000 crore a year in the race to capture the market, while workers toil for little money, paid by the hour or minute, with no security. Gig workers cannot hold gate meetings, but on New Year's Eve 2025 a mass log-off became their strike. Companies impose discipline through ratings and by shutting accounts, which the writer sees as a kind of lockout.

The Centre's four labour codes replaced 29 laws and recognised gig workers on paper, but the schemes have still not reached the ground and the trade unions' objections were brushed aside. After a strike in January, quick commerce companies had to drop the promise of delivery in ten minutes. The writer asks whether this turn by the Congress is for show or a real change, and says that tipping the balance from big capital towards workers needs far more political will.
nazar: Insurance and rest spots are needed, but the gig worker's real fight is with the algorithm, which can shut his account without giving a reason. Until there is a right to be heard when an account is shut and a guaranteed minimum income, welfare schemes will stay incomplete.
The Noida arrests and the delivery workers' log-off are two parts of the same story. Whether the worker is in a factory or on an app, the right to organise is his strongest shield.
sawal: Will a one per cent fee stop the algorithm doing as it likes?
ref: Gig workers
People paid per task or delivery through a digital platform, such as food delivery riders or cab drivers; they are usually not given the status of employees.
Labour codes
The central government's four codes (wages, industrial relations, social security, occupational safety) that replaced 29 old labour laws; unions see them as anti-worker.

h: A burqa behind the laughter: 'Salma Deewani' and an old template
dek: In ThePrint, Mariam Hasan writes that this character from 'India's Got Latent' may be funny, but she hardens the very assumptions about Muslim women whose weight they carry every day.
body: On Samay Raina's show 'India's Got Latent', Bhagyashree Tarke's character Salma Deewani is a married woman from Hyderabad's old city: two children, a husband working in Dubai, difficult in-laws and a crush on Salman Khan. Mariam Hasan says the whole sketch is built from the same markers by which popular culture has identified the Muslim woman for years.

Tarke created the character in 2015 at the National School of Drama as a fifteen-minute solo play, drawing on the women of old Hyderabad she grew up among. In 2019 it became a full play and was staged about 45 times, including in Sri Lanka and Dubai. On stage Salma wears a burqa. Tarke calls it satire on lonely, frustrated lives inside the four walls of the home.

The writer accepts that non-Muslim performers can play Muslim characters, but playing an identity and feeding the assumptions attached to it are different things. Tarke takes off the costume after the show; Muslim women cannot. The burqa, suppressed desire and family background turn into guesses about their education, freedom and choices, which follow them from the classroom to the office. They are put either in the box of the oppressed or in that of the 'exception'.

Hasan grants Salma her quick wit, especially the line that a woman who swears gets a bad name and a man does not, a double standard found in every community. But the father who pulled her out of school after Class 10, the 'useless' men of the house, and Raina's joke 'cousin means husband?' all repeat the same old template, although marriage between cousins is not limited to Muslims. In her view the act gives no reason to look beyond the veil; it only makes a familiar stereotype more entertaining.
nazar: At a time when Muslim women's clothes and education are the stuff of politics, and classroom doors shut over the hijab, even laughter on stage is not innocent. Satire should aim at the powerful, not at people who already live under suspicion.
The answer is not censorship but more voices: Muslim women writing, performing and telling their own stories, so that audiences are not left with a single character.
sawal: The costume comes off on stage; why does the stereotype reach the classroom?
ref: India's Got Latent
Comedian Samay Raina's online talent show, in which contestants and judges joke freely; the show has been in controversy over its content before.
Stereotype
A ready-made, simplified idea about a community that is pinned on every individual and lays the ground for discrimination.

h: COP31's collapse is not a failure: it is the system's real face
dek: In Al Jazeera, Ilan Kapoor writes that the Antalya summit ended without an agreement because climate talks are built so that a clash with oil and gas interests keeps getting put off.
body: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, ended on Sunday without any shared agreement. The draft put before about 200 countries did not even name fossil fuels. The European Union and several Pacific island nations rejected it, while oil-producing countries held out against strong language. It is the first time since 2009 that talks have broken down like this.

According to Ilan Kapoor, who teaches at York University in Toronto, this is no accident. Under the Paris Agreement each government sets its own target, there is no obligation to stop new oil and gas projects, and the consensus rule hands every stubborn country something like a veto. There was not even agreement on carrying out the promise made at COP28 in Dubai to move away from coal, oil and gas.

The writer believes the real tug of war is outside the conference hall. Producer countries protect their income and clout, consumer countries depend on cheap energy, and governments shield voters from the immediate cost. The draft put its faith in carbon removal technologies, which he calls a trade of political relief today for an uncertain benefit tomorrow.

The bitterest point is about money. A proposed target of 120 billion dollars for adaptation was dropped from the revised draft. The countries that have done least to heat the planet are the ones facing drought, floods and displacement, and they are borrowing to cover the damage. According to the writer this is not charity but accountability for damage done by an unequal world economy.

He suggests that rich countries first stop new fossil fuel expansion, give money for adaptation and loss and damage as grants, not loans, and that the most vulnerable countries get more say in decisions. Multilateral forums should survive, but faster coalitions and domestic laws should move alongside them, or everyone's participation will become everyone's delay.
nazar: For South Asia this is not distant diplomacy. Coastal villages on the Bay of Bengal, Himalayan rivers and the flood-hit areas of Pakistan are paying the price of this delay. Cutting adaptation money means poor countries will have to build dams and embankments out of their school and hospital budgets.
Countries like India will also have to think about how forcefully they can demand accountability from rich countries while defending their own dependence on coal.
sawal: Under whose pressure was the 120 billion dollar adaptation target dropped?
ref: COP (Conference of the Parties)
The annual meeting of the member countries of the UN climate treaty, where decisions on cutting emissions and climate finance are taken by consensus.
Adaptation finance
The money countries need to protect themselves from effects such as floods, drought and rising seas, for things like embankments, drought-resistant farming and warning systems.

h: Bangladesh loosens its rules at the shipbreaking industry's request
dek: In The Daily Star, Ahmedul Karim Chowdhury warns that under industry pressure Bangladesh lowered the environmental category of ship recycling and distanced itself from the Basel Convention, a price workers and the coast will pay.
body: On 29 September the Bangladesh government took two decisions on the same day, and according to reports both came at the request of shipbreaking yard owners. The first moved the industry from the 'red' to the 'orange' category under the Environment Conservation Rules 2023, meaning somewhat lighter scrutiny. The second chose a path of stepping away from the provisions of the Basel Convention and relying only on the Hong Kong Convention.

Ahmedul Karim Chowdhury, who is associated with the Bangladesh Maritime University, accepts that the industry matters: it supplies scrap steel, employs thousands, and yard owners have put big money into meeting standards. Their complaints about delays and double approvals deserve a hearing. But hearing them is one thing, and handing the rules over to them is another.

According to the writer, the two conventions are not two versions of the same rule. The Hong Kong Convention, in force since June 2025, deals with certification of yards, an inventory of hazardous materials and inspection. The Basel Convention requires prior notice and consent for the movement of hazardous waste across borders. Basel's member countries still do not accept that the Hong Kong Convention gives equal protection, and in the writer's view there is no legal route for partly leaving Basel either.

The danger is not on paper. Asbestos, oil residue and heavy metals go straight into coastal land and water. The deaths of 10 workers from toxic gas at the Ferdous Steel yard in Sitakunda show that a certificate is no guarantee of safety in everyday work.

The writer wants the government to make public the legal and technical basis of both decisions, to set up a time-bound digital system for approvals, and to have worker representatives, experts and coastal communities sit in on future reviews.
nazar: Shipbreaking is the clearest picture of the world's inequality: ships from rich countries come to die on the shores of Chittagong, Alang and Gadani, and their poison settles in the lungs of poor workers. Every decision to loosen the rules pushes this burden further down.
Gujarat's Alang is in the same race. If neighbouring countries lure ships by cutting rules, it will become a race to the bottom, and everywhere the losers will be the workers.
sawal: Why were the rules not tightened after 10 workers died in Sitakunda?
ref: Basel Convention
A 1989 international treaty that requires written consent and safe disposal before hazardous waste is sent from one country to another.
Hong Kong Convention
The International Maritime Organization's treaty on the safe and environmentally sound recycling of ships, which came into force on 26 June 2025.

h: Whose pain is called 'trauma', and whose is just news?
dek: In Dawn, Muna Khan asks why in the Western world even minor discomfort is given the status of trauma, while proof is demanded for the devastation in Gaza, Sudan and Congo.
body: In 2017 Muna Khan, a Karachi journalist and journalism teacher, was studying at a foreign university. There, before difficult texts, students were warned that they could skip them if they wished, so that no one's old wounds would be reopened. The writer noticed that this gentleness was sincere but did not reach far. The history of the Global South or of Muslims became a topic for debate, while the experiences of others were wounds to be cared for.

In this context she takes up the debate around a new book by American professor Catherine Liu. Liu argues that trauma has become a kind of currency for the educated professional class. When everyone's pain is called equal, the politics of poverty and exploitation is easily pushed aside, and being recognised becomes a substitute for justice.

Liu sees one root of this trend in Oprah Winfrey's public confession in 1986, which gave courage to many victims but also turned pain into a brand. Today this can be done with a phone, and the benefit goes to whoever has a platform, a polished story and the right audience.

This is where the writer's real question begins. For more than two years the people of Gaza have been recording their own destruction on their phones: children pulled from rubble, parents writing names on their children's arms. Yet their videos are doubted, the death toll is debated and grief is called propaganda. According to one reviewer, the word Palestinian appears only once in Liu's book.
Muna Khan adds geography to Liu's argument about class. She does not ask that the word be dropped, only that each time we ask for whom it is being used and who is being kept out.
nazar: This question applies to our own media too. One accident in a big city is debated for weeks, while the suffering in Manipur's relief camps or of Sudan's refugees stays a headline for a day or two. Sympathy too is handed out according to the map of power.
As long as the language for recognising suffering remains the property of a few, bombing far away will stay a statistic and inconvenience close by will be a tragedy.
sawal: Doubt for Gaza's videos, so why trust for our own pain?
ref: Trigger warning
A warning given before a text, film or other material that it contains violence or distressing scenes, so the reader or viewer can be prepared or skip it.
Global South
The countries of Asia, Africa and Latin America that went through colonialism and are still counted at the margins of the world economy.

h: Bengal SIR: hear the appeals of deleted voters first
dek: The Supreme Court told the tribunals to put on hold appeals against names being added and to hear first those whose names were struck off, with priority for the Kolkata Municipal Corporation area.
body: On Monday the Supreme Court gave a clear direction to the appellate tribunals set up after the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral roll in West Bengal: split the appeals into two parts. On one side are people whose names were removed from the roll; on the other, appeals filed to oppose someone's name being added. There is no hurry over the second kind, so they should be put off for now.

A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V. Mohana said the appeals of deleted voters in the Kolkata Municipal Corporation area should be settled first, because civic elections are due there soon. The Election Commission was told to consult the Calcutta High Court to increase the number of tribunals and find places for them in different parts of the city.

Appearing for the petitioners, Prashant Bhushan told the court that of about 38 lakh appeals, only around one lakh have been decided so far, and 93 per cent of those have gone in favour of the deleted voters. According to him, in the Kolkata municipal area alone more than two lakh people are off the roll and their appeals are pending.

Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan pointed out that the Commission's own affidavit shows the state's Chief Electoral Officer has himself filed appeals against names being added. He argued that this amounts to the Commission appealing before an appellate officer it appointed itself, which has no basis in law. After this the bench proposed holding back such appeals.
nazar: When the deleted name turned out to be right in 93 per cent of the appeals heard, this is not a slip in the pruning; it is a verdict on the way the pruning was done. The court has set the right priority, but the real question remains: why should lakhs of people, most of them poor and migrants, run from office to office to get their own names back, and who will hold accountable the officer who filed appeals the other way?
sawal: Who will question the officer who appealed against names being added?
ref: SIR

Special Intensive Revision: the Election Commission's drive in which the electoral roll is checked afresh. In this round there have been allegations of large-scale deletion of names in several states.
Appellate tribunal
A body that hears challenges to decisions to delete or add names. In Bengal these have been set up under the Supreme Court's supervision.

h: Bhusawal: 14,562 requests to delete names, only 74 found valid
dek: When bulk Form 7 applications in a BJP-held seat in Maharashtra were checked, nearly all of them turned out to be baseless, and the administration has begun legal action against those who filed them.
body: In the Bhusawal Assembly seat of Jalgaon district, 14,562 Form 7 objections were filed to get names removed from the electoral roll. After checking, only 74 names were found fit to be removed. Maktoob reported this citing a report in The Indian Express. The seat is held by BJP MLA Sanjay Savkare.

The Congress had complained that 186 people filed these applications in bulk. After the complaint, the district administration began legal action against those people, whose intent it itself called 'malicious'. As soon as the matter came up, 21 applicants withdrew their 2,532 objections. The rest were asked for evidence and booth level officers checked every name on the spot.

According to the report, this case is not isolated. It is alleged that during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral roll, BJP booth agents in many places used Form 7 to get Muslim voters' names deleted. On 30 October the Supreme Court had asked the Election Commission to take corrective steps on bulk applications in Uttar Pradesh, and had ordered an inquiry into fake applications in Delhi's Mustafabad.

The Chief Electoral Officers of Telangana and Karnataka have also ordered action on the misuse of Form 7. Maktoob also notes that in some states people left out by the SIR are facing difficulties with benefits such as rations and with renewing passports.
nazar: When fewer than one in a hundred applications turn out to be valid, this was not a misunderstanding but a planned campaign. In Bhusawal there was a complaint and a check, so the names were saved; but where no party or group was watching, how many people may have quietly dropped off the roll? Checking every bulk Form 7 application and punishing those who file false ones should be the rule, not the exception.
sawal: Where there was no one to complain, how many names were cut?
ref: Form 7
An application to object to a name on the electoral roll or get it removed. Any voter can file this objection against someone else's name.
Booth Level Agent (BLA)
Workers appointed by political parties who keep watch on the electoral roll work at each booth.

h: Chhatarpur: Dalit women carry their lotas to the SP's office
dek: Dalit women of Richhara village allege they are stopped from offering water at a new temple and from filling water at a government hand pump, and that threats continue even after a case of assault was registered.
body: Some Dalit women from Richhara village in Madhya Pradesh's Chhatarpur district reached the Superintendent of Police's office carrying the lotas (small brass pots) they use for the Kartik holy bath. They said they were not asking for any special favour, only for what the rest of the village already has: the right to worship and to fill water.

The family alleges that they are not allowed to offer water at the new Shiva temple built in the village, and that there are objections when they go to fill water at the government hand pump or well. According to them, insulting songs are sung in front of their daughters and daughters-in-law, and they are even told off over things like riding a mare at weddings or wearing shoes.

Lota Ahirwar, fifty, alleges that on 18 November, in a quarrel over water, some people from the village beat her and abused her by caste. After a complaint at Bhagwan police station, a case was registered against four people under the SC/ST Prevention of Atrocities Act, but the family says that since then they have been getting threats, such as being run over with a tractor.

The women asked the SP for action against the accused, protection for the family, and to be able to go to the temple and hand pump without fear. The report records no response from the police or the district administration, and it is also not clear what has happened in the case so far.
nazar: If 76 years after the Constitution came into force a government hand pump in some village still gives water by caste, this is a failure not just of the village but of the administration. Registering a case is not enough; giving the family protection and equal access to the temple and hand pump is the police's direct responsibility.
sawal: Whose duty is it to enforce equality at a government hand pump?
ref: SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act
A 1989 law that makes caste insults, violence and boycott against Dalits and Adivasis a crime and provides for special courts.
Article 15
The provision of the Constitution that bars discrimination on the basis of caste and gives everyone equal rights to use public places such as wells and tanks.
photo_note: Villagers going to market, Amrita Sher-Gil; representative image

h: Video of CRPF officer on bodies in a dumper turns out to be fake
dek: An Alt News check found that the viral video of the CRPF's Special DG was made by putting a fake voice over real footage.
body: The bodies of two Special Police Officers (SPOs), Bobby Chand and Rashpal Kumar, killed in an attack in Kishtwar in Jammu and Kashmir, were taken to their village Kiyar in a dumper truck, without coffins. NDTV reported this on 14 November and there was great anger about it in the area.

In this climate an 18-second video spread in which CRPF Special Director General Sandeep Khirwar is supposedly heard saying that all the military vehicles in the area were busy, so a dumper was used. From 16 November many accounts on X and Facebook spread it, saying the army had refused to provide an ambulance.

Alt News traced the original footage from the ANI logo on the video. In that statement, given in Srinagar, Khirwar speaks of the remains of the missing SPOs being found, of honouring the martyrs and of justice for the families; there is no mention of a dumper. The pictures are the same, but the voice and the way of speaking are different. An AI detection tool put the chance of a synthetic voice in the clip at 98.9 per cent.
On 17 November the CRPF's Srinagar sector also said from its official handle that the video had been tampered with and that the words attributed to Khirwar were made up.
nazar: Questions about the real news of bodies being sent in a dumper needed to be asked, but cashing in on that anger with a faked voice weakens the real question itself. Clips made with AI are becoming a weapon in every side's hands; the answer is to ask real questions with real evidence.
sawal: Who answered for sending the bodies of slain SPOs in a dumper?
ref: SPO
Special Police Officer: local people hired on a small honorarium to assist the police. In Jammu and Kashmir they are often the most at risk.
Deepfake audio
Using AI to copy someone's voice and put in their mouth words they never said.

h: Non-bailable warrant against Dhruv Rathee in an eight-year-old defamation case
dek: A Delhi court issued the warrant over a 2018 video that accused the BJP IT cell of offering a bribe to a witness.
body: A Delhi court on Monday issued a non-bailable warrant against YouTuber Dhruv Rathee in a 2018 defamation case. The order was passed by Judicial Magistrate Anam Rais Khan. Newslaundry reported this citing a Bar and Bench report.

The complaint is by Vikas Sankrityayan alias Vikas Pandey, who calls himself a supporter of the Prime Minister and runs a social media page called 'I Support Narendra Modi'. In his May 2018 video, Rathee had alleged that Pandey was part of the BJP IT cell and that through a middleman he offered fifty lakh rupees to a man named Mahavir Prasad to withdraw his allegations of spreading fake news.

At the time, Delhi Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal had retweeted the video. Pandey filed a defamation case against both of them. In October his lawyer told the court that Rathee mostly lives abroad, so summons could not be served on him for years.
The court had earlier issued a bailable warrant and in October accepted a plea for an early hearing. The next hearing is on 3 December. The report records no response from Rathee or his lawyers.
nazar: It is the very law that treats defamation as a crime that creates a situation where an arrest warrant can come out over a video eight years later. Appearing in court is everyone's duty, but the sword of criminal defamation hanging over those who speak and criticise is not good for democracy.
sawal: Should defamation still be a crime today?
ref: Non-bailable warrant
A court order under which the police arrest the accused and produce them in court; bail cannot be given at the police station, only the court decides.
Criminal defamation
In India defamation is a civil matter and also a crime, with a punishment of up to two years. There have long been demands to remove it.

h: High Court quashes suspension of 16 Kalady students
dek: The Kerala High Court said the Sanskrit university's disciplinary inquiry did not follow natural justice, and the students must be allowed back into classes at once.
body: On Monday Justice P.V. Kunhikrishnan of the Kerala High Court quashed the suspension of 16 students of Sree Sankaracharya University of Sanskrit, Kalady, and ordered that they be allowed back on campus and in classes immediately. A separate exam was ordered within six weeks for the ten students who missed their exams.

The matter goes back to 13 August, when the students went to meet the Vice Chancellor during a Syndicate meeting. Their complaints were: 27 vacant lecturer posts, delays in certificates, poor infrastructure and stalled fellowships. After a clash with the police two FIRs were filed, and on 1 September all 16 students, who are linked to the SFI, were suspended.

The court found that the charges were stated neither in the suspension order nor in the notice for the hearing. Witness statements, including an online statement by the Vice Chancellor, were recorded in the students' absence; they were given neither copies of the complaints nor a chance to cross-examine. The inquiry committee also dug up old, unrelated complaints. The court rejected the argument that the students should go to the university's own grievance bodies, calling it 'an appeal from Caesar to Caesar's wife'.

The university may hold a fresh inquiry by the rules, but there will be no fresh suspension in the meantime. The students had already been suspended for 84 days. Higher Education Minister Rojy M. John, who had favoured making an apology a condition, said he would respond later.
nazar: Keeping students out for three months without telling them the charges, when they had come with complaints about vacant posts and stalled fellowships, was not discipline but punishment. The court reminded us that the right to be heard does not end at the campus gate. Universities owe students who ask questions answers, not demands for apologies.
sawal: When will the 27 vacant lecturer posts be filled?
ref: Natural justice
A basic principle of law: before punishing someone, tell them the charges, hear their side and have the decision made by an impartial person.
Speaking order
An order that sets out the reasons for the decision and discusses the evidence, so that it can be challenged.

h: Sonam Wangchuk joins the fast in Leh, demanding winter polls be put off
dek: As soon as he was freed from house arrest, Wangchuk joined the Leh Apex Body's fast, while the Home Ministry has signalled that talks will come after the elections.
ask: Postpone the 4 December elections, grant a legislature and the Sixth Schedule
body: The protest in Ladakh took a new turn on Saturday. As soon as he was released from house arrest, climate activist Sonam Wangchuk joined the hunger strike of the Leh Apex Body (LAB). He appealed directly to the Prime Minister and the Defence Minister to step in, and said that isolating people in this sensitive border region is not good for national security either. According to him, many villages have announced a boycott of the elections and some polling stations have been removed.

LAB president Chering Dorjay Lakruk alleged large-scale deletion of voters' names. Sajjad Kargili of the Kargil Democratic Alliance said many voters with the same name were listed at one polling station and asked for an inquiry. The groups say that holding elections in November and December, amid bitter cold and seasonal migration, means shutting out students, workers and first-time voters.

The administration argues that heated polling stations have been arranged and that timely elections will strengthen grassroots democracy in the new districts. The Home Ministry has signalled that talks with the High Powered Committee could resume between 5 and 10 December, that is, after the Hill Council elections. The LAB and the KDA have rejected this timetable.
nazar: Putting the talks after the elections sends the message that the people of Ladakh will be asked their opinion after the decision is made. In a region where the report of the judicial inquiry into the 2025 violence has still not come out, the way to win trust runs through postponing the elections and open talks, not through ignoring those on fast.
sawal: Whose voice will a vote cast in the freezing cold become?
ref: Leh Apex Body and KDA
Two joint platforms of religious, political and social groups of Leh and Kargil. Since 2021 they have together been demanding statehood and the Sixth Schedule for Ladakh.

h: Clash over coal block survey in Dumka's Badalpara, 12 police personnel hurt
dek: A gram sabha (village assembly) called for a Haryana power company's proposed mine turned violent; the villagers' side has not yet come out.
ask: No survey or drilling for the proposed coal mine
body: Late on Sunday night villagers and police clashed over a proposed coal mine in the Badalpara-Kalyanpur area, under Shikaripara police station in Jharkhand's Dumka district. The coal block has been allotted to Haryana Power Generation Corporation Limited (HPGCL). A company team had come to the village for a gram sabha meeting on the survey and development of the mine.

According to the police, they were told that protesters had taken a member of the survey team hostage. Stones and sticks are alleged to have been used against the police who went to free him. Station in-charge Amit Lakra said at least 12 police personnel were injured, two of them with head wounds. The company's general manager, Sagar Singh Meena, alleges that he was beaten and thrown into a water-filled pit, and that local people took him to hospital on Monday morning. According to Deputy Development Commissioner Aniket Sachan, the trouble began during the gram sabha.

The police have begun an investigation. According to other reports, raids are being carried out in nearby villages and extra forces have been deployed in the area. Why the villagers oppose the mine is not recorded in any report.
nazar: Violence cannot be defended, but the biggest gap in this story is that no one is writing down what the villages of Santhal Pargana, whose land is to go, have to say. In a Fifth Schedule area, the gram sabha is a place for consent, not a formality for passing the mine's agenda. Before the raids, someone should listen to what the village was saying.
sawal: A gram sabha with no room to say 'no': whose assembly is it?
ref: PESA Act
A 1996 law that gives the gram sabha in Fifth Schedule Adivasi (indigenous) areas key powers in decisions on land, forests and minerals.

h: Rayagada's Pujari Bambu village sits in at the collectorate: give us a road
dek: An Adivasi village that has lived without a paved road for seven decades has given three days' notice, warning that otherwise it will send a plea for mercy killing.
ask: Let the government give us a road or take our lives
body: On Monday the people of Pujari Bambu, an Adivasi-majority village in Baising panchayat of Odisha's Rayagada district, walked about six kilometres to the district headquarters and began an indefinite satyagraha (non-violent sit-in) outside the collectorate. Men, women and schoolchildren carried the tricolour and placards saying the government should give them a road or take their lives.

The villagers say that since Independence they have not had an all-weather road, which keeps hospitals, schools and government schemes out of their reach. Just last week two seriously ill patients were carried across the Nagavali river in makeshift slings. The Rural Development department has even surveyed the 4.76 kilometre route.

Balaram Panda, who is leading the protest, alleges that even after the survey, block officials sent a wrong report and stalled the work, and that memorandums sent to everyone from the sarpanch to the Chief Minister have come to nothing. The protesters have given the administration three days. After that they will send a plea for mercy killing to the President through the Collector and march to the Chief Minister's office in Bhubaneswar. The report records no response from the administration.
nazar: That a village has to talk of a mercy killing plea for a road of under five kilometres shows that in Odisha's Adivasi areas even basic rights are stuck in files. Corridors for carrying minerals get built fast; a village road does not get built even after a survey.
sawal: How long must a village that carries its sick in slings wait?
ref: Nagavali river
A river that rises in the Kalahandi region of southern Odisha and flows through Rayagada into Andhra Pradesh. In the rains it cuts off the way to many Adivasi villages.

h: Adivasi students protest in Imphal: release the stalled scholarships now
dek: About 35,000 Scheduled Tribe students have still not received their 2025-26 scholarships, and the students took to the streets after their ultimatum ran out.
ask: Release the pending ST scholarships at once and pay them on time in future
body: Scholarships for Scheduled Tribe students in Manipur have been stuck for months, and on Monday students gathered against this outside the Directorate of Tribal Affairs and Hills in Imphal. The protest was organised jointly by the All Colleges Tribal Students' Union Imphal (ACTSUI) and the Tribal Youth Council Manipur. Students held placards and raised slogans for the scholarships to be released without delay.

According to the groups, the scholarships for the 2025-26 session were sanctioned in April 2026 itself, but the money did not reach the accounts of about 35,000 students. On 17 November they had set a deadline of 21 November and said that if the money did not come, the protest would intensify from 23 November. Some protesters also demanded the resignation of Deputy Chief Minister and Tribal Affairs Minister Nemcha Kipgen and of the department's director.

The students say the minister told their union that the amount had already been sent to the directorate. The police kept things calm by talking to them on the spot. No detailed statement has come from the department or the government.
nazar: In a Manipur that has been through violence and displacement, a scholarship is a condition for poor hill students to keep studying, not a prize. The minister says the money was sent, the students say it never came; the account of the file in between should be made public.
sawal: In which drawer did the sanctioned money lie for seven months?
ref: Post-matric ST scholarship
A joint central and state scheme that pays the fees and living costs of Scheduled Tribe students studying after Class 10.

h: Home Guards protest in Patna, demand an account of EPF and pension benefits
dek: Bihar's Home Guard personnel marched from Gandhi Maidan to their headquarters and said their EPF has not been deposited in several districts since 2019.
ask: Retirement benefits from the date of joining, deposit the pending EPF
body: On Monday Bihar's Home Guards gathered near Patna's Gandhi Maidan and marched in a procession to the Home Guard headquarters at Chhajjubagh. There they sat in protest outside the office of the Director General cum Commandant General. The protest was called by the Bihar Rakshavahini Swayamsevak Sangh, and a large number of personnel took part.

According to the Sangh's general secretary Sudeshwar Prasad, the most serious issue is the EPF (Employees' Provident Fund). He alleges that in some districts deductions have been made since September 2019 but the money has not been deposited, which is hurting the insurance and pension of retired personnel and the families of those who have died. Their demands are that retirement benefits be counted from the date of joining, including the earlier period of cash payment, that dependants of deceased personnel get jobs on compassionate grounds, and that alleged irregularities in deputation stop.

Prasad said these points had been put forward many times, in writing and in person, but there had been no concrete action, and not even a date for talks at headquarters had been fixed. He warned that if needed, the sit-in would turn into a bigger movement. The officials' response is not recorded in the report.
nazar: Home Guards carry the police's load during elections, festivals and floods, but their job is still left incomplete under the label of 'volunteer'. If money deducted from their pay did not reach their accounts for years, this is not just an administrative slip; it is a case of theft of their labour.
sawal: Where was the deducted EPF stuck for seven years?
ref: Home Guards
A volunteer force that spread across the country after the 1962 war with China, which assists the police and is paid an allowance for each day of duty.

h: Farmers put off their sit-in at NTPC gate in Greater Noida for now
dek: Farmers from 24 villages affected by the Dadri project handed the administration a court order on higher compensation and paused their protest on an assurance.
ask: Pay the higher compensation as the court ordered
body: Farmers from 24 villages in Greater Noida affected by NTPC's Dadri project had announced an indefinite sit-in at the project gate from 25 November. On Monday they put it off for now. According to the headline of the report, the sit-in has been postponed until 15 December. The decision came after the district administration and NTPC officials assured them that the farmers' problems would be resolved.

A delegation led by Bharatiya Kisan Union Manch district in-charge Ajab Singh Bhati, district president Akshay Mukhiya and western Uttar Pradesh president Krishan Bhadana met District Magistrate Medha Roopam and ADM (Administration) Sanjay Singh. The farmers handed the administration the court order on higher compensation. They are demanding that the higher compensation be paid and that other problems pending for years be solved.

Bhati said plainly that the farmers will not give up their rights and that if no solution is found in the set time, the protest will start again. The report does not say what exactly the administration promised.
nazar: When a court has already ordered higher compensation and farmers still have to threaten a sit-in to get it carried out, it shows how sluggish the system is. The date of the assurance will need watching.
sawal: Why should a sit-in be needed to get a court order carried out?
ref: NTPC Dadri
NTPC's coal and gas based power station in Gautam Buddh Nagar district. Land from nearby villages was taken for it, and disputes over compensation have gone on ever since.

h: A boy who survived exploitation goes back to Nigeria to find his mother
dek: In an Al Jazeera Witness film, Sosa Henkoma, an activist who came through trafficking and gang exploitation in Britain, travels to Nigeria to look for a trace of his missing mother.
body: This film in Al Jazeera's documentary series Witness was made by Sameer Modi. At its centre is 27-year-old Sosa Henkoma, who is today a well-known activist in Britain against human trafficking and the exploitation of children. The film takes him on a journey he had put off for years: the search for his mother.

Sosa was born in Nigeria but brought up in Britain. His bond with his mother was broken when he was very young. According to the film's introduction, his mother set out many years ago trying to reach Europe and was never heard of again. Where she went, what happened on the way, whether she is alive: these questions remain unanswered to this day.

Sosa's childhood in Britain was not easy. The film's description says he suffered abuse at home and outside, gang violence and exploitation. As a teenager he came into contact with criminal gangs and became part of one himself. According to a report in the Marathi newspaper Navarashtra, he also went to jail, and later the authorities accepted that he had in fact been a victim of trafficking and exploitation, not a criminal.

That turning point changed the direction of his life. From a gang member he became an effective activist working among young people, who stresses that children pushed into crime need protection before punishment.

In Nigeria Sosa meets relatives on his mother's side and tries to piece together clues from hazy memories and scattered information. According to the film, the search soon turns into a bigger question: what is identity, where is home, and which forces shaped the lives of both mother and son through migration.

The route from West Africa to Europe, which often runs through the Sahara and Libya to the Mediterranean, has for years been counted among the deadliest migrant routes in the world, and the families of thousands who went missing on it are still waiting for answers. The film's introduction does not say whether Sosa found any firm news of his mother; that answer comes only by watching the film.
nazar: Sosa's story shows that trafficking and migration are not separate issues. When safe ways to cross borders for a living are shut, people are handed over to agents and deadly routes, and the children left behind become easy prey for exploitation.

It is a mirror for India too: from girls taken from Jharkhand and Odisha to the big cities to workers trapped abroad, the habit of treating the victim as a criminal is common here as well. The question is one of protection, not punishment.
sawal: Who will correct the mistake of treating an exploited child as a criminal?
ref: Witness

Al Jazeera English's long-form documentary series.
It shows grounded stories by independent filmmakers from around the world.
Grooming

Winning a child's trust and slowly preparing them for sexual or criminal exploitation.
In Britain the issue is also linked to gangs using children.

h: A young poet looks for his grandmother's hands in cow-dung cakes
dek: Ravi Yadav's five poems look at the village home, the tiled roof, birds and women's labour with the fine eye of memory.
body: Ravi Yadav studied at Delhi University and BHU and is now doing research at Lucknow University. Sammukh has published five of his poems together, and nearly all of them stand on the same ground: a home in some village of the east, which is slowly turning into memory.

The first poem is about women patting cow-dung into cakes in the afternoon sun. The poet looks for the touch of his late grandmother in the fingerprints left on the cakes. The mahua tree, the veil and the courtyard soaked in rain keep this poem from being only a fond picture; it becomes a record of labour that was never even counted as work.

'Phurguddi' (a small bird) is a poem about a tiny, restless bird that keeps coming and going through the house, from the pond to the kitchen. The grinding stone, lentils, rice left on the threshold and the songs of mother and grandmother make a world here in which people and birds lived together. 'Khaprail' (tiled roof) remembers the roof of that same house, under which a big family and many birds were raised and the walls leaked in the rains. The poem also points towards the tradition of Awadhi folk poetry.

'Karmua ke Phool' (flowers of the karmua) is a scene of a pond's purple and green colours and a woman catching fish, where light turns ordinary labour into magic. The last poem, 'Pratiksha ke Phool' (flowers of waiting), dwells on the last moments of a life: an unfinished sweater, an empty glass, sunlight sliding down a wall.
The strength of these poems is their stillness. The poet does not make noise; he names things and tries to save them.
nazar: Patting cow-dung cakes, splitting lentils, pounding paddy: this uncounted labour of village women is recorded neither in GDP nor in most literature. Ravi Yadav's poems look at it with nostalgia but also with respect, and that is what makes them worth reading.
sawal: Whose labour do the handprints on the dung cakes bear witness to?
ref: Phurguddi
A name used in the dialects of eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar for a small bird, often the prinia or a similar little hopping bird.

h: Black holes, the veto and love: five poems by Preeti Chaudhary
dek: Political science professor Preeti Chaudhary reads the loneliness of love in the language of physics and international politics.
body: Preeti Chaudhary teaches political science at Dr Ambedkar University in Lucknow. She went from village and small-town schools to BHU and JNU, and her book 'Deh Dhare Ko Dand' (the price of having a body) has already come out. Her five untitled, numbered poems published on Sammukh are about love, but their language is borrowed from books of science and politics.

The introduction mentions a neutron star, as if to say that the difficulties of mathematics and physics are light next to the weight on the heart. In the first poem the old image of the sea and the fish is turned upside down: here the waves are not support but a net, and the speaker has hung a 'No Entry' board on her heart.

The second poem is the longest. A woman who cannot understand the arithmetic of relationships counts what she has given up: evening tea, the seasons, the patience of waiting. She has climbed mountains alone, and her one wish is to see Kanchenjunga turn golden in the morning. The third poem is short and sees happiness as a morning stream passing through a forest, which pauses a little and moves on.

In the fourth poem love is a black hole from which there is no return, and the question is whether falling was fate or the result of one's own faith. The fifth is the most political: one side armed with weapons and myths, the other unarmed, growing meaningless as it keeps repeating the call for disarmament. The poet compares this to the veto in the Security Council.

This blend of private grief and public language in these poems is not new, but it is fresh. Linking the unequal power inside a relationship to the hypocrisy of international treaties saves the poems from becoming mere songs of separation.
nazar: Power inside the home and power in the world run on the same grammar; feminism has been saying this for years. Preeti Chaudhary makes it sting more by placing it in the cold vocabulary of the veto and disarmament.
sawal: Why in love does the burden of disarming always fall on one side?
ref: Veto
The right of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council, by which any one of them can single-handedly block a resolution.

h: Kumaon's daughters, Allahabad's Coffee House and Shivani's sulk
dek: The fifth part of Mrinal Pande's memoir begins with hill women being uprooted again and again and goes on to Allahabad University in 1962.
body: Senior journalist and fiction writer Mrinal Pande is writing her memoir on Jankipul under the title 'Bhakhai Akath Katha Birtant' (telling the untellable tale). The fifth part, 'Ghar Bahar-Deredari' (home, away and camping), begins with the habit of Kumaon's hill Brahmin families of moving from one place to another. According to the writer, the real price of this moving was paid by women: daughters were married off early, and the family trees recorded only the history of men.

Then the story turns to her mother, who never accepted staying silent. In an in-law household that kept purdah, to mock the educated daughter-in-law she was told to split lentils by hand, so she sent for an old servant. The days in Jhansi, her brother's house in Orchha where the writer was born, and a funny episode involving a basket of jalebis are all written with a light touch.
In between comes a deeper point: for a daughter every home is a temporary stop, and the duties of mother, daughter and daughter-in-law go with her until she dies.

In 1962, in the middle of the war with China, the writer left Nainital and arrived at Allahabad University. She shows the changing face of that city: convent schools shunning Hindi, a growing love of English-medium schooling even among Hindi writers, and open debates between left and right camps at the Coffee House. Firaq, Nirala, Mahadevi and Amrit Rai's family are characters in this world.

At the end there is a lovely story. The two sisters persuaded 'Diddi' to give a happy ending to Shivani's novel 'Chaudah Phere' (fourteen rounds), then being serialised in Dharmayug, and afterwards Shivani kept complaining that the girls had hijacked her story.
nazar: A woman's name missing from the family tree seems a small thing, but this is how history gets written by half. Mrinal Pande's memoir is an attempt to record that missing half: her mother's defiance and her daughters' uprooting.
sawal: Who kept erasing daughters' names from the family trees?
ref: Shivani
Gaura Pant 'Shivani' (1923-2003), popular Hindi fiction writer and Mrinal Pande's mother. 'Chaudah Phere' and 'Krishnakali' are among her best-known novels.

h: The restlessness of drifting from poetry and coming back: Vallari Srivastava's poems
dek: The poems of Vallari Srivastava, a poet who seldom publishes, are about writing, wandering and not turning away from the truth.
body: Jankipul has published six poems by Vallari Srivastava. The moderator's short introduction says she has been shy about getting her work published, and also recalls a scholar's remark that poetry is a way of thinking. These really are thinking poems, mostly about her own writing.

The first poem shows a lost person the way: grass grown over the scars of war, the evening after the noise, boats resting on the shore, sunlight filtering through trees. Nature here is a refuge, not a sermon. In the second poem the speaker has drifted away from her poetry, the way a villager is pulled towards the city. The ink dries, the roots crack, but the sun comes back every day, and so does the hope of return.

The third poem sees poems themselves as wandering guests who knock on the door at night, stay a while and then go off to some other reader's home. The fourth trusts in the discipline of writing, leaving fireflies and shadows behind, just as a farmer trusts his crop.

The last two poems are sharper. One asks a kindred spirit whether they too love art more than show, and sets the image of Gandhari's blindfold against deliberately shutting one's eyes. The other is about someone who gave up their pen, picked up a bag and hid their head in the sand like an ostrich.
The language is simple, the images are homely, and in places the poems explain more than they need to. Still, there is an honest restlessness in them that reaches the reader.
nazar: Gandhari's blindfold and the head in the sand: both images sting the writer of today in particular, when silence has been made the safest choice. Vallari Srivastava's poems are a reminder of the pen's integrity.
sawal: When does a writer give up the pen and pick up a bag?
ref: Gandhari
In the Mahabharata, the wife of Dhritarashtra, who tied a blindfold over her eyes to share her blind husband's lot. Today the image is also used for deliberately looking away.

h: Bollywood's Dorian Gray: Samit Basu's new novel
dek: According to Sayari Debnath's review on Scroll, 'The Pictures of Darpan Ray' is a dark but entertaining satire on fame, the obsession with youth and the changing times of the film industry.
body: Samit Basu's new novel 'The Pictures of Darpan Ray' is loosely inspired by Oscar Wilde's 'The Picture of Dorian Gray', but it is set in the Mumbai film industry. Sayari Debnath has reviewed it on Scroll.

The story begins in 2004, when three young Bengalis arrive in Mumbai: the handsome Darpan, who wants to be a hero, and his friends Rishi and Diya, who want to write and make films. A director on the slide 'discovers' Darpan and renames him Vikram Rai, because a Bengali accent and his old name are not thought right for a star.

In four parts the novel covers a journey of twenty years. A shoot on an island in Thailand, where the friends get ahead by rewriting the script; then the 2018 period, when #MeToo, streaming and corporate capital changed the industry; and finally a future in which writers and actors begin to seem useless next to AI. Along the way there are also a billionaire's wedding, mysterious deaths and vanishing stars.

According to the reviewer, Basu's real subject is the fragility of fame and the obsession with youth and beauty, an industry that values the body more than talent. Darpan accepts this easily, while Rishi and Diya struggle with their work being undervalued. Nepotism and the commercialisation of cinema are also targets.

Debnath finds the novel fast-paced and entertaining, and says Basu's own past experience as an insider makes the shooting section feel real. She recalls a time when Bollywood was willing to bet on outsiders.
nazar: Doors closing on outside talent, the market's command and now the shadow of AI: Basu's satire is not only about Bollywood but about every kind of creative work that is being made into a part in the profit machine.
sawal: When the face is what sells, what room is left for the writer?
ref: The Picture of Dorian Gray
Oscar Wilde's 1890 novel, in which the hero stays young forever while his portrait grows old and ugly with his sins.

h: The language of freedom in Faiz, Sahir and 'Do Bigha Zamin'
dek: Neera Chandhoke's new book explores what freedom means in the idea of India through political theory, Bombay cinema and progressive Urdu poetry.
body: Writer Madhulika Liddle has reviewed political scientist Neera Chandhoke's new book 'Languages of Freedom' (Speaking Tiger) on Scroll. She begins with Rousseau's 'Social Contract', according to which a person must give up part of their individual freedom in exchange for the collective freedom of a just society. Chandhoke's question is the same: how one person's freedom collides with another's and with society as a whole.

The book has five essays. The first reads Gandhi's swaraj (self-rule) alongside the ideal societies of Plato, Thomas More and Tolstoy. The second enters the debate over 'us' and 'them' through Aurobindo Ghosh and K.C. Bhattacharya and asks what Indian culture really is; the answer stresses diversity and a shared heritage.

The third and fourth essays are described as the most readable. They examine the Urdu poetry that came out of the Progressive Writers' Association and IPTA, and Hindi cinema, which carried the ideas of secularism, equality and freedom to ordinary people. Faiz, Sahir, 'Pyaasa' (the thirsty one) and 'Do Bigha Zamin' (two bighas of land) serve as examples here. The fifth essay surveys Indian political thought by way of Rammohan Roy and Vivekananda.

Liddle feels that the second and fifth essays are heavy and call for slow reading. But she praises Chandhoke's clear language and balance, both between India and the West and between theory and concrete examples. Chandhoke values Gandhi's non-violence, but also criticises him for resting the national movement on Hindu symbols.
According to the reviewer, the book's central fear is that a narrow ruling class could pawn even our freedom to think. So she calls it a timely book, unsettling and at the same time encouraging.
nazar: At a time when a shared heritage is viewed with suspicion, it is necessary to remember that the Indian idea of freedom was shaped not only in the Constituent Assembly but also in Faiz's poems and in the eyes of Bimal Roy's farmer.
sawal: Can today's cinema ask a question like 'Do Bigha Zamin' did?
ref: IPTA
The Indian People's Theatre Association, a left-wing cultural body formed in 1943, with which artists such as Balraj Sahni, Khwaja Ahmad Abbas and Salil Chowdhury were associated.
Progressive Writers' Association
A writers' organisation founded in Lucknow in 1936 under the presidency of Premchand, which tied literature to social change.
